question: NPC: Before we begin — programs in brief
intro: Ada the Chief Artificer pulls up a stool by the forge. “No experience needed. Here are the few words you will meet in the next hour.”

steps.say: A **program** is a list of exact instructions. The computer carries them out one at a time, from the top down. This program has two instructions. It shows Forge lit, and then Anvil ready.

beats.say: A **program** is a list of exact instructions. The computer carries them out one at a time, from the top down.
This program has two instructions. It shows Forge lit, and then Anvil ready.

check.prompt: Swap the two lines, so the Anvil ready line comes first. What does the computer show first now?
check.why: Instructions run in the order they are written, top to bottom. Whichever line comes first finishes before the next one starts.

steps.say: You write Java as **source code**: plain text in a file that ends in .java. A **compiler** translates that text into **bytecode**: instructions for the **Java Virtual Machine** (JVM), the program that runs them.

beats.say: You write Java as **source code**: plain text in a file that ends in .java.

steps.say: Java begins at a method called **main**. Inside it sit **statements**: single instructions that each end with a **semicolon**. The semicolon is the full stop of a statement. Java is picky: leave one out and the program will not compile.

check.prompt: How many statements are inside main in this program?
check.why: Each println line is one statement, and each ends with a semicolon. There are three.

outro: “That is enough to start. Now show me what you remember.”

question: Which description best fits a computer program?
correct: Written instructions that the computer carries out one after another
incorrect: A written goal that the computer works out its own steps to reach
Written instructions that the computer carries out all at the same moment
A list of questions the computer asks you before choosing what to do
feedback: A program is a list of exact instructions, and the computer follows them in order, top to bottom, one at a time. It does not work out the steps for itself: you have to spell out every one. Order matters too, which is why the same lines in a different order can give a different result.

question: Java's motto is “write once, run anywhere”. What makes that possible?
correct: The compiler makes bytecode, which any computer with Java can run
incorrect: The compiler makes a separate copy for every kind of computer
Java programs are sent over the internet each time they run
Java programs are written in plain English, which all computers read
feedback: You write Java in a .java file. The compiler turns it into bytecode, saved in a .class file. Any computer that has Java installed — Windows, Mac, Linux, a phone — can run that same bytecode. You do not have to rewrite or rebuild anything for each kind of machine.

question: When a Java program starts running, the first method it carries out is the one named ___.
feedback: Execution starts in a method named main, written in lowercase. The classic form, which works in every Java version and which you will see everywhere, is public static void main(String[] args). Java 25 also accepts shorter forms such as void main(). Either way the name is what Java looks for.

question: Most Java statements have to end with one particular symbol, much as a sentence ends with a full stop. That symbol is ___.
feedback: The semicolon marks where one statement stops, the way a full stop ends a sentence. Leave it out and the compiler refuses the whole file with the message ';' expected. A line that opens a block with { (the main line, an if, a loop) does not take one, because the block's closing } does that job.

question: Which line compiles and prints the text Hello, world! on the screen?
feedback: Text has to sit inside double quotes. Single quotes are for exactly one character, so 'Hello, world!' is rejected, and with no quotes at all Java tries to read Hello and world as names of things it has never heard of. Java is also case-sensitive: System needs its capital S, and a lowercase system is simply not found.

question: What does this program show on the screen? Type it exactly.
feedback: print writes its text and stays on the same line; println writes its text and THEN moves down to a new line. So 25 lands directly after Java. Nothing adds a space for you either: Java prints exactly the characters between the quotes, so the result is Java25 and not Java 25.

steps.say: A **variable** is a named box that holds one value. This line makes one: int is the variable's **type**: this box holds whole numbers. arrows is its name, and = puts 10 inside.

check.why: Right side first, using the value in the box now, which is 7 and no longer 10. 7 + 5 is 12, and 12 replaces the 7.

steps.say: There are no quotes around arrows, so Java prints what is in the box. That is the whole trick: one box per variable, right side first, and the newest value wins.

outro: “The next monster has a box of its own, called coins. Follow it line by line, exactly as we just did.”

feedback_template: Follow the box one line at a time. coins starts at {{a}}. The second line works out {{a}} + {{b}} and stores {{mid}}. The third line starts from that NEW value, not from the original one: {{mid}} - {{c}} leaves {{expected}}, and that is what println shows.

question: Which of these lines correctly create a variable and put a first value in it? (Select all that apply)
feedback: The pattern is type, name, a single =, value, semicolon. var is a legal stand-in for the type: Java sees the 1 and works out int for itself. A doubled == asks “are these equal?” instead of storing anything, so it cannot create a variable. A name may contain digits but may not start with one. And "3" in quotes is text, which does not fit in an int box; write 3 without the quotes.

question: Every variable has a type, which says what kind of value it holds. Match each value to the type of variable it belongs in.
feedback: int is for whole numbers, such as an age. double is for numbers with a decimal point, such as a price. String is for text, which always sits in double quotes. boolean holds only true or false, written without quotes.

question: Write the statement that creates an int variable named lives holding the value 3.
feedback: Type, name, =, value, semicolon: int lives = 3;. Java is case-sensitive, so Int or Lives would be different words, and the number has no quotes because quotes would turn it into text. var lives = 3; is accepted as well, since Java works out the type int from the 3.

question: A program contains the line  int n = 4;  Match each print statement that comes after it to what appears on the screen.
feedback: Quotes are the whole difference. Inside double quotes, Java prints the characters exactly as typed and never looks inside any box, so "n" is just the letter and "n + 1" is just those five characters. Without quotes, n means “the value in the box”, and n + 1 is worked out first and then printed. None of these lines changes n: it still holds 4 afterwards.

question: The + sign joins text to whatever is beside it. What does this program print?
feedback: name and age have no quotes, so Java uses what is in those boxes: Ada and 18. The piece in quotes, " is ", is printed exactly as typed, spaces included. + glues the three together, left to right, into one line of text.

question: Arrange these lines, first to last, so that the program prints 14.
feedback: The box has to exist before anything can use it, so the int line comes first, and println comes last so that it shows the finished value. The middle is where order matters: adding first gives 7 and doubling that gives 14, while doubling first gives 10 and adding gives only 12. Same lines, different order, different program.

question:
Both numbers here are whole numbers. What does result hold?
int result = 7 / 2;
feedback: When Java divides one whole number by another, it keeps only the whole part and drops the rest: 2 fits into 7 three times. It does not round up to 4. To keep the half you would write 7.0 / 2, which gives 3.5. (The 1 is the remainder, which is what 7 % 2 gives.)

question: Java follows the same order of operations as school arithmetic. What does this print?
feedback: Multiplication is done before addition, so 3 * 4 is worked out first: 12. Then 2 is added, giving 14. Going strictly left to right would give 20, which is wrong. To add first, use parentheses: (2 + 3) * 4 is 20.

question: A program wants to ask the user for their age and read what they type. Which tool does Java provide for that?
feedback: A Scanner reads what the user types: input.nextInt() reads a whole number, and input.nextLine() reads a line of text. System.out and println go the other way — they send text OUT to the screen. String is a type for holding text, not a way of reading it.

question: What does this program print?
feedback: An if guards only the lines inside its own braces. 3 > 5 is false, so Java skips from the { to the matching } and Strong is never printed. The last line sits outside the braces, so it runs whatever the test said. An if does not stop the program; it only decides whether its own block is carried out.

prompt: Fill in the two missing words so that this program prints  Rich!  exactly once and then moves to a new line.
feedback: if checks its test once and carries out the block once when the test is true, which is what “exactly once” needs. A while in that spot would check again after every pass, and since gold never changes, 12 > 10 would stay true and Rich! would pour out forever. println, with the ln, is the one that moves to a new line afterwards; print leaves the cursor where it stopped.

question: NPC: Either this, or that
intro: Nia stands at a fork in the corridor with a lantern in each hand. “An if on its own can only do something or do nothing. Usually a program wants to do one thing or the other.”

steps.say: Here is an **if** with an **else**. Each has its own **block**: the lines between a pair of braces. When the test is true, the first block runs. When it is false, the else block runs.

steps.say: The test in the round brackets is a **comparison**, and its answer is true or false. Java has six of them. Notice that “equal to” is two equals signs. A single = is the one that puts a value in a box.

check.prompt: Which of these asks whether score is exactly 100?
check.why: == compares. A single = would store 100 in score, and >= would also be true for 101 and everything above it.

outro: “The next monster has a fork of its own. Work out the test first — true or false — and only then look at the blocks.”

question: Work out the test first, then pick the block. What does this program print?
feedback: 4 >= 10 is false, so the first block is skipped and the else block runs. With an if-else exactly one of the two blocks runs each time: the first when the test is true, the else when it is false.

5 and 10 are different numbers, so a != b (“not equal”) is true and a == b (“equal”) is false. 5 is less than 10, so a < b is true. That makes both a > b and a >= b false: 5 is neither greater than 10 nor equal to it.

question: A while loop repeats its block for as long as its test is true. What does this program print? (Put each number on its own line.)
feedback: Follow the box. number starts at 1: 1 <= 7 is true, so 1 is printed and number becomes 3. Then 3 and 5 are printed the same way. When number is 7, 7 <= 7 is still true, so 7 is printed too. Then number becomes 9, the test is false, and the loop stops.

question: This program uses a variable, a loop and an if together. What does it print?
feedback: The loop runs with i as 1, then 2, then 3, and each pass adds the current i to the box: total goes 0, 1, 3, 6. The println is not inside the loop, so nothing appears while it is running. After the loop, 6 > 5 is true, so the if lets its block run and the finished total is printed once.

question: Every finished quest earns a bonus of 5 points. Return the score with the bonus added.
hint: One line: the word return, then the score plus 5.
feedback: score arrives already holding a value, so there is nothing to set up: work out the answer and hand it back with return. The whole body is one line.

question: The bridge troll takes a toll of 3 coins, but only from travellers carrying more than 10. Return how many coins the traveller has left.
hint: Change coins inside an if, then return coins after the closing brace so that both kinds of traveller get an answer.
feedback: The if changes the box only when its test is true; the return sits after the closing brace, so it runs either way. Exactly 10 is not more than 10, so that traveller keeps everything.
